sec.title: Background
sec.p: The orally available toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) agonist prodrug RO7119929 is converted to active drug predominantly in the liver, where it is hypothesized to reprogram the local immune microenvironment. We aimed to explore the safety, pharmacokinetics (PK), and preliminary antitumor activity and obtain the proof-of-mechanism for RO7119929 in patients with liver cancer.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: RO7119929 was investigated in mouse tumors and liver tissue from cynomolgus monkeys. In the first-in-human, open-label, dose-escalation and expansion study, patients with histologically confirmed advanced or metastatic primary liver cancers or solid tumors with predominant liver involvement received RO7119929 weekly in 3-week cycles either on a flat-dose (FD) or step-up dose (SUD) schedule.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Preclinical results demonstrated antitumor activity and the proinflammatory proof-of-mechanism in mouse liver tumors and cynomolgus monkey liver tissue. The subsequent first-in-human study enrolled 27 patients in five FD dose-escalation cohorts, 18 patients in a FD dose-expansion cohort, and 9 patients in two SUD dose-escalation cohorts. The most common primary tumor type at study entry was hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (31%). PK data showed fast conversion of RO7119929 to the active TLR7 agonist. Treatment-related adverse events (TRAEs) were observed in 50 (91%) patients across all treated patients; the most commonly reported TRAE was cytokine release syndrome (CRS) in 48 (81%) patients. CRS was also identified as a dose-limiting safety risk and had a dose-dependent incidence and severity. Grade 3 CRS occurred in six (13%) patients receiving FD RO7119929, while no grade 3 CRS was reported in SUD patients at comparable target dose levels. TLR7-related transient, dose-dependent gene expression and cytokine induction was observed both with FD and SUD treatment and corresponded with treatment-induced local inflammation of the tumor microenvironment induced by reprogramming of the myeloid cells. Among 17 patients with HCC, one durable complete response was observed, and 10 (59%) patients had stable disease.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: SUD appears to reduce the risk of CRS while maintaining mode-of-action-relevant pharmacodynamic effects. The clinical activity of RO7119929 as a single agent was limited, suggesting that combination therapy with a checkpoint inhibitor may be needed to leverage the proinflammatory potential of RO7119929 and further increase antitumor activity.

sec.title: WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPIC

list-item.p: The clinical use of toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) agonists for the treatment of cancer is hampered due to systemic immune activation leading to dose-limiting toxicities.

The TLR7 agonist prodrug RO7119929 is converted to its active drug predominantly in the liver (1), and is hypothesized to reprogram the local immune microenvironment by cytokine induction (2) and secondary attraction of effector T cells to the tumor environment (3).

Treatment with single-agent RO7119929 induced local inflammation via myeloid cells both in animal models and patients with advanced or metastatic primary liver cancers or solid tumors with predominant liver involvement.
Step-up dosing reduced the risk of cytokine release syndrome while maintaining mode-of-action-relevant pharmacodynamic effects in patients.

sec.title: HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICY

list-item.p: Combination therapy with a checkpoint inhibitor may be needed to further increase antitumor activity.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Cancer immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitor (CPI) monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) such as programmed cell death protein-1/programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) and cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-associated protein 4 (CTLA-4), has substantially improved treatment outcomes, particularly in patients with immunogenic or inflamed tumors. However, more than 80% of eligible patients do not respond to treatment with CPI mAbs or eventually develop resistance.1,3 To increase the number of patients who respond to immunotherapy, immune cell-activating compounds may help to generate a proinflammatory tumor microenvironment (TME) and sustain immune responses.

Toll-like receptor 7 (TLR7) agonists have been shown to stimulate innate immune cells, leading to the activation of humoral and cellular immunity, thereby inducing a series of antitumor activities.4 Imiquimod is approved for the topical treatment of the skin of patients with superficial basal cell carcinoma.5 However, when given systemically, TLR7 agonists have shown only modest clinical activity, mainly due to systemic immune activation leading to dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs).6,8

RO7119929 is a prodrug that is primarily converted in the liver to the active drug RO7117418.9 Based on the prodrug design, we hypothesized that RO7119929 via RO7117418 stimulates TLR7 positive cells predominantly in the liver and tumor, resulting in high levels of immunostimulatory cytokine release at the site of liver tumors while reducing systemic immune activation. Consequently, we hypothesized that such a promotion towards an inflammatory TME fosters T cell activation and subsequent antitumor immunity.

Here we present results from the non-clinical and clinical investigation of RO7119929. The non-clinical investigation aimed to demonstrate antitumor activity and the proof-of-mechanism in mice liver tumors and cynomolgus monkey liver tissue. The clinical investigation took place in a first-in-human, phase 1 dose-escalation and expansion study that assessed the safety, pharmacodynamics (PD), pharmacokinetics (PK), and preliminary antitumor activity of single-agent RO7119929 given orally to patients with unresectable advanced or metastatic primary liver cancers and other solid tumors with predominant liver involvement.

sec.title: Non-clinical methods and materials
sec.p: Methods and materials to evaluate the effects of RO7119929 on peripheral cytokines and tumor and liver tissue in a HEP55.1c mouse model and cynomolgus monkeys as well as on human peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) are described in online supplemental material S1.

sec.title: Study design and objectives
sec.p: WP41377 is a first-in-human, open-label, multicenter, multiple-ascending dose-escalation and dose-expansion phase 1 study. The primary objectives of the study were to evaluate the safety and tolerability and to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) and/or optimal biologic dose of single-agent RO7119929. The primary study endpoints were DLTs and incidence of adverse events (AEs). Secondary objectives included the evaluation of the PK profile of RO7119929 and RO7117418 (active drug), biomarkers in peripheral blood, and the preliminary clinical activity of RO7119929.

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: The main inclusion criteria were: male or female aged ≥18 years; unresectable advanced or metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), biliary tract cancer, or solid tumor with hepatic metastases; measurable disease with at least one measurable locally untreated liver lesion, as defined by Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors (RECIST) V.1.1; Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance score 0 or 1; and life expectancy of ≥12 weeks. There was no limit on the number of prior antineoplastic regimens received. Patients were excluded if they had a history or clinical evidence of central nervous system primary tumors or metastases, or evidence of extrahepatic primary tumor or metastasis requiring prompt medical intervention or were receiving treatment with systemic immunosuppressive medication. Details are provided in the protocol (online supplemental file 2).

sec.title: Intervention and dose escalation
sec.p: RO7119929 was administered weekly (QW) in 3-week cycles. RO7119929 capsules were administered orally using three schedules. Details regarding the dose cohorts are provided in online supplemental figure S1. Treatment duration was up to 12 months or until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, or withdrawal of consent, whichever occurred first.

Within Schedule 1 (flat-dosing (FD)), RO7119929 was administered QW at the same dose in 3-week cycles. The starting dose for the dose-escalation was 1 mg. The DLT period consisted of the first 3 weeks (ie, the first cycle). The sequential dose increases were guided by a modified continual reassessment method (mCRM) dose-escalation with overdose control (EWOC) model based on the occurrence of DLTs (further details are provided in online supplemental material S2). At least three evaluable patients were enrolled in each cohort.

Within Schedule 2 (step-up dosing (SUD)), RO7119929 was administered QW in 3-week cycles with SUD during cycle 1. The dosing step at Cycle 1 Day 1 was fixed at a dose level with minimal risk of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) grade ≥2, while the dosing step at Cycle 1 Day 8 was fixed at a dose with an acceptable dose-toxicity profile guided by safety information in the FD cohorts. The target dose at Cycle 1 Day 15 was determined using an mCRM-EWOC design and was then administered QW during each subsequent cycle. The DLT period consisted of the first 4 weeks.

Within Schedule 3, RO7119929 was also administered QW in 3-week cycles. Tocilizumab was administered intravenously as pretreatment on Cycle 1 Day 1, approximately 2 hours prior to RO7119929 administration. The DLT period consisted of the first 3 weeks.

sec.title: Safety assessments
sec.p: All AEs were reported from initiation of study treatment until 60 days after the last study treatment. The severity of AEs was graded according to National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events criteria V.5.0. A DLT was defined as a grade ≥3 AE or laboratory abnormality (online supplemental material S2) that (1) occurred during an assessment period of 3 weeks (FD) or 4 weeks (SUD) from the start of the first cycle; (2) was not attributed to disease progression, concomitant illness, or another clearly identifiable cause.

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics and exposure response analyses and modeling
sec.p: Intensive PK sampling was done up to 30 hours after the first (Cycle 1 Day 1) and fourth RO7119929 dose (Cycle 2 Day 1) in the FD cohorts, and after the third (first target dose; Cycle 1 Day 15) and fourth RO7119929 dose (Cycle 2 Day 1) in the SUD cohorts. RO7119929 (prodrug) and RO7117418 (active drug) concentration data were assessed using validated methods. Non-compartmental PK analysis of RO7119929 and RO7117418 and population PK and PK/PD and PK/safety models are described in online supplemental material S3.

sec.title: PD/biomarkers
sec.p: Peripheral blood for PD assessments was collected from all participants. In addition, paired tumor biopsies taken from the hepatic tumor manifestations were mandatory for patients enrolled into the expansion cohort. An immunohistochemistry duplex assay against Ki67 and CD8 and single-nuclei RNA-sequencing (snRNA-seq) was performed as described in online supplemental material S4.

sec.title: Antitumor activity
sec.p: Measurable lesions were assessed up to 28 days before and then every 6 weeks after the initiation of treatment. Patients who permanently discontinued study treatment without radiologically defined progression continued tumor radiological assessments until they experienced disease progression or started a new anticancer therapy. Tumor response was evaluated according to RECIST V.1.1.10

sec.title: Statistical considerations
sec.p: The safety analysis included all patients who received at least one dose of study treatment. For the inclusion in the PK and antitumor activity analysis, an on-study PK sample and tumor assessment was required, respectively. To be evaluable for DLTs, participants needed to have taken in all doses scheduled within cycle 1. Participants experiencing a protocol-defined DLT already with fewer doses were also DLT-evaluable.

No formal sample size calculation was performed, approximately 35–40 patients each were estimated to be enrolled for dose-escalation, and up to 60 additional patients for dose-expansion in up to three cohorts.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the data for safety, PK parameters, and peripheral blood and tumor PD markers. For the evaluation of preliminary antitumor activity, objective response, and disease control rates were summarized using relative frequencies and 90% confidence limits.

sec.title: Non-clinical results
sec.p: To assess the peripheral activity of RO7119929, we treated mice with Hep55.1c liver cancer tumors with a single dose of 1, 3, or 10 mg/kg of RO7119929. The profiling of interferon-alpha (IFN-α), interleukin-6 (IL-6), tumor necrosis factor–alpha (TNF-α), and IP-10/CXCL10 showed that these peripheral cytokines peaked after 2 hours in a dose-dependent manner (figure 1A). Cytokine levels returned to baseline 12 hours after dosing. As it has been described that repeated dosing of TLR7 agonists can result in tachyphylaxis,11 we evaluated the dosing frequency (figure 1B). QW dosing with RO7119929 resulted in the continuous induction of IFN-α, whereas every other day or daily dosing resulted in lower or no IFN-α induction. IL-6 induction was highest after the first dose of the QW regimen and subsequently, in contrast to IFN-α, declined over time. When administered every other day or daily, the IL-6 levels consistently decreased to approximately one-third of the level after the first RO7119929 dose. Based on these data, we chose a QW dosing regimen for subsequent mouse studies, toxicology studies in cynomolgus monkeys, and for the first-in-human clinical study to ensure consistent induction of the mode-of-action-driving cytokine IFN-α by RO7119929.

sec.p: We tested the antitumor efficacy of RO7119929 in the Hep55.1c liver cancer model as described by Hage et al,12 with and without checkpoint inhibition targeting PD-L1 (figure 1C). In this model, Hep55.1c murine tumor cells were implanted by intrahepatic injection and monitored using a contrasting agent by QW microcomputed tomography scans. Although RO7119929 monotherapy demonstrated antitumor efficacy in this model, combination with an anti-PD-L1 antibody enhanced efficacy in intrahepatic tumors, suggesting that RO7119929 would be suitable for combination with CPI for further clinical development.

To better understand the gene expression changes induced by RO7119929, we assessed Hep55.1c tumors in mice and cynomolgus monkey healthy liver tissue after in vivo exposure by bulk RNA sequencing (figure 1D,E), as well as human healthy donor PBMC exposed to the active TLR7 compound RO7117418 by single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) (figure 1F). For RNA-seq in mice, we chose two time points, an early one at 30 min (to assess the direct effects of TLR7 stimulation) and a later one at 6 hours post-treatment. In comparison to the rather mild effects on the RNA level at 30 min, RO7119929 resulted in a strong induction of genes associated with IFN-α cytokine signaling at 6 hours post-treatment (figure 1D). Induction of interferon-stimulated genes (ISGs) was consistently observed in all three species. Of note, we obtained the cynomolgus monkey data after the fifth dose of RO7119929, indicating that the QW dosing regimen allowed for the induction of type I IFNs after multiple dosing. In addition, the induction of ISGs was dose-dependent, with the strongest induction observed at the highest dose (0.75 mg/kg). To further characterize direct and long-term in vivo effects induced by RO7119929 treatment at the level of distinct cell types, we also performed scRNA-seq in Hep55.1c tumors at 6 hours after treatment with RO7119929 on days 1 and 13, in the absence or presence of anti-PD-L1 (figure 1G–I and online supplemental figure S2). Our analysis focused on T cells and myeloid cell populations, which were the predominant immune infiltrates in the tumors (figure 1G and online supplemental figure S2A).

The strongest differences in gene expression were apparent at the 6 hours time point on day 1, when type I IFN-related genes were strongly upregulated, but hundreds of genes were also significantly differentially expressed on RO7119929 and RO7119929+anti-PD-L1 treatment at day 13 (online supplemental figure S2B–D). We found that RO7119929 induced T cell activation via increased expression of genes such as Gzmb, Ctl4, and Ifng. Increased Gzmb gene expression occurred both at 6 hours and day 13 in both RO7119929 treatment groups, but not in the anti-PD-L1 group, when compared with control treatments. While Ifng, Ctla4, and also Foxp3 expression was transiently upregulated at 6 hours following RO7119929 treatment, this effect was not sustained at day 13. Conversely, Ki67 upregulation was only noted at day 13 post-treatment, and was significant exclusively in the RO7119929+anti-PD-L1 group (figure 1H). When looking at the myeloid cells specifically (figure 1G), we observed a switch from M2-like towards M1-like macrophage signatures on treatment with RO7119929 alone or in combination with anti-PD-L1. We observed an increase in M1 macrophage-related gene expression,13 14 with individual genes such as Cxcl10 or Il4i1 showing transient upregulation (only at 6 hours), while others such as Cd300e or Isg15 were upregulated even after repeated administration of RO7119929 (figure 1H,I and online supplemental figure S2D). While individual M2 macrophage-related genes15 16 such as Trem2, Mrc1, and Cd209a showed significant downregulation, the trend was not consistent across the distinct signature genes. These changes were observed predominantly in animals treated with RO7119929 alone or in combination with anti-PD-L1, but not in the anti-PD-L1 group (figure 1H–I and online supplemental figure S2D).

sec.title: Clinical results from the first-in-human study of RO7119929
Patients
sec.p: Between July 2020 and April 2022, the first-in-human study of RO7119929 enrolled 55 eligible patients at eight study sites in five countries (three sites in Spain, two in the Republic of Korea, one each in Denmark, Hong Kong, and Taiwan). The FD part of the study included 45 patients: 27 in five dose-escalation cohorts and 18 in a dose-expansion cohort. Two SUD dose-escalation cohorts included a total of nine patients. An additional study cohort, in which a single dose of tocilizumab was given as pretreatment before FD treatment with RO7119929, enrolled a single patient. Online supplemental figure S1 provides details of the patient disposition. Patient enrollment was stopped on February 1, 2022, following a decision by the sponsor to stop further development of RO7119929 based on a portfolio reprioritization. Consequently, no further patients were enrolled in the SUD part of the study and the tocilizumab pretreatment cohort.

The median age of the 55 enrolled patients was 59 years (range: 37–77 years) (online supplemental table S1). The number of Asian (51%) and white (49%) patients was similar. The most common primary tumor type at study entry was HCC (31%); 11 of 45 (24%) patients in the FD cohorts, 5 of 9 (56%) patients in the SUD cohorts, and the patient who received tocilizumab pretreatment had this diagnosis (online supplemental table S1). Most patients (86%) had received at least two prior lines of systemic therapy.

The median treatment duration was 5.3 weeks (range: 0.1–55.9) for the FD cohorts, and 10.1 weeks (range: 0.1–26.1) for the SUD cohorts (online supplemental table S2). 54 of the 55 patients discontinued treatment, 46 (85%) due to progressive disease or symptomatic deterioration (online supplemental figure S1).

sec.title: Safety flat-dosing
sec.p: In the first part of the study, patients received FDs of 1, 3, and 9 mg RO711992 in the first three dose-escalation cohorts, and 4 and 6 mg RO7119929 in two subsequent cohorts. A total of five DLTs occurred in 2 of 4 patients in the 9 mg cohort and 2 of 10 patients in the 6 mg cohort. All four patients had grade 3 CRS starting within approximately 3–5.5 hours after dosing on day 1 as a DLT. One patient in the 6 mg cohort also had an abnormal grade 3 liver function test 15 hours after dosing on day 1 as a DLT. No formal MTD was established by the mCRM-EWOC model due to insufficient information.

Based on the dose-escalation results, we chose a dose of 5 mg RO7119929 for a dose-expansion cohort that enrolled 18 patients. Of the 45 patients in the FD dose-escalation and dose-expansion cohorts, 44 (98%) experienced AEs. Online supplemental table S3 lists frequent AEs irrespective of relatedness.

40 of the 45 treated patients (89%) had at least one AE of CRS, of which 34 patients (85%) presented with mild or moderate CRS. All AEs of CRS were considered related to treatment. Per the protocol, all events with clinical presentation of CRS (including isolated symptoms such as fever) were to be reported using the preferred term “cytokine release syndrome”.

Other treatment-related AEs included nausea (13%), aspartate aminotransferase increased (11%), and asthenia, chills, and lymphopenia (9% each). A total of 14 (31%) patients had at least 1 grade 3 or 4 treatment-related AE (table 1), the most common of which were CRS (13%), lymphopenia (9%), and aspartate aminotransferase increased, alanine aminotransferase increased, and platelet count decreased (4% each).

sec.p: Six patients (13%) had an AE that led to the withdrawal of treatment, four due to grade 3 CRS (DLT, mandated per protocol), one each due to grade 3 blood bilirubin increased and grade 2 infection. A total of 24 patients (53%) died during the study, 23 patients due to progressive disease, and 1 patient due to cerebral effusion (occurring ≥90 days after the last RO7119929 administration, not deemed related to study drug). No AE leading to death was reported.

The proportion of patients with a grade 2 or 3 CRS event increased with the dose (figure 2A). Most CRS events occurred within treatment cycles 1 and 2, with a trend towards lower grades of CRS or no CRS with repeated dosing (figure 2C). The time to onset of CRS symptoms was generally within a few hours after dosing (online supplemental table S4). All CRS events resolved during the study. Fever symptoms and hypotensive episodes generally resolved within 12 and 24 hours after dosing, respectively. Except for grade 3 CRS, CRS events were managed with routine interventions such as paracetamol, fluids, and corticosteroids (online supplemental table S5). Six patients received tocilizumab for CRS management, and two patients with grade 3 CRS were admitted to the intensive care unit for monitoring.

sec.p: The patient who received a single dose of tocilizumab pretreatment before treatment with an FD of 4 mg RO7119929, experienced grade 1 CRS after receiving RO7119929 in cycle 5.

Patients with HCC experienced slightly more grade 2 and 3 CRS events than patients without HCC (7/11 (64%) patients vs 19/34 (56%) patients). CRS events of grade 3 severity were specifically observed in the subgroup of patients with HCC and liver disease resulting from non-infectious causes (5/7 patients vs 0/4 patients with liver disease resulting from viral infections), but patient numbers were small and group sizes were unbalanced.

sec.title: Safety step-up dosing
sec.p: A SUD schedule was explored based on the results of the FD cohorts suggesting that severe CRS occurs only in the first cycle, and supporting non-clinical (see above) and clinical PD/biomarker and PK/PD modeling data (see below). In the first SUD cohort, patients received an initial RO7119929 dose of 2 mg on day 1, followed by a dose of 5 mg on day 8, which was also the target dose given on day 15 and for subsequent RO7119929 administrations (schedule 2/5/5 mg). As no DLTs were observed in four patients treated, a second cohort explored a schedule with a target dose of 6 mg (schedule 2/5/6 mg). No DLTs were observed in the five patients treated in this cohort.

All nine patients in the SUD cohorts experienced AEs. Frequent AEs are listed in online supplemental table S3. Seven (77.8%) patients had at least one AE of CRS, which was generally considered related to treatment with RO7119929 (table 1). Nausea in two patients (22.2%) was the only other treatment-related AE that was reported for more than one patient. Treatment-related AEs with a grade 3 or 4 severity (alanine aminotransferase increased, aspartate aminotransferase increased, lymphopenia, and vomiting) occurred in one patient (11.1%) each. Similar to the FD schedules, most CRS events occurred within treatment cycle 1 and 2 (figure 2B). However, patients in the SUD cohorts appeared to experience fewer cases of grade 2 CRS (22% with SUD vs 71% with FD at comparable target doses) and no grade 3 CRS (figure 2D).
None of the SUD patients had an AE leading to treatment discontinuation. One patient died during the study due to progressive disease.

sec.title: Clinical activity
sec.p: Of the 52 patients who had at least one tumor assessment after the start of treatment, 28 patients (54%; 95% CI 39.5% to 67.8%) had progressive disease as best overall response, and 23 patients (44%; 95% CI 30.5% to 58.7%) stable disease. 10 of the latter patients were patients with HCC (4 of 11 patients with HCC in the FD cohorts, 5 of 5 patients with HCC in the SUD cohorts, and the patient who received tocilizumab pretreatment) (online supplemental figure S3).

One patient in the 6 mg dose-escalation cohort experienced a complete response (online supplemental figure S4). This patient had HCC with Barcelona Clinic Liver Cancer (BCLC) B stage at study entry, with two target lesions and multiple non-target lesions in the liver, and had received three prior lines of systemic treatment including a CPI. The patient experienced CRS grade 2 after receiving the first 6 mg dose of RO7119929, followed by CRS grade 1 in subsequent treatment cycles. Alpha-fetoprotein levels declined starting at cycle 3 (online supplemental figure S4). The patient had stable disease at the first tumor assessment at week 6 and partial response at week 12. A complete response was reached at week 42 and was ongoing at the last assessment at week 60 (online supplemental figure S4).

sec.title: Pharmacokinetics
sec.p: Following QW administration of oral RO7119929 as single agent in the FD and SUD cohorts, time to maximum concentration (Tmax) values of RO7119929 ranged from approximately 0.5 to 4 hours, with a median of 1 hour (online supplemental figure S5, online supplemental tables S6 and S7). The estimated elimination half-life of RO7119929 was approximately 1–2 hours, indicating rapid prodrug conversion to the active drug, RO7117418. The plasma concentration of RO7117418 increased rapidly and reached its peak level (Cmax) between 1 and 6 hours (median Tmax of 2 hours) after dosing (online supplemental tables S8 and S9). RO7117418 exposure, Cmax and area under the curve (AUC)0–inf, showed an approximately dose-proportional increase in the tested dose range with linear elimination. The PK of RO7117418 was well described by a two-compartment model with first-order, non-linear absorption, and linear elimination (online supplemental material S3). The derived effective half-life of RO7117418 was 3.1 hours.

sec.title: Blood PD results and PK/PD modeling
sec.p: ISG15, IFN-α, IL-6, and CXCL10 chemokine (not shown) downstream of TLR7 were measured in the plasma as a PD readout of RO7119929 after administration of the first RO7119929 target dose (first dose for FD cohorts or third dose for SUD cohorts) (figure 3A). After both FD and SUD treatment, cytokines were induced in a transient, dose-dependent manner at doses >1 mg, whereas ISG15 levels appeared to reach saturation at doses ≥4 mg. The IFN-α and ISG15 levels observed in the FD cohorts were maintained in the SUD cohort. In contrast, SUD led to relatively lower IL-6 levels compared with the FD cohorts at the same target doses (5 or 6 mg RO7119929). PK (RO7117418)/PD (ISG15) indirect response Emax modeling suggested a maximum median ISG15 induction fold change of around 100, which was approached at doses >4 mg RO7119929 (figure 3B). While doses >4 mg RO7119929 would result in similar maximum ISG15 responses, higher RO7119929 doses were predicted to result in more sustained ISG15 levels over time (figure 3B). A modest and transient induction of TLR7 was observed in the peripheral blood in a non-dose-dependent manner (online supplemental figure S6).

sec.title: Exposure-safety (CRS) analysis
sec.p: Exposure-safety analysis based on FD data revealed a strong relationship between PK, IL-6, and CRS grade ≥2 after the first dose of RO7119929 (figure 4). The predicted risk of CRS grade ≥2 at 2 mg was estimated to be 2.26% (95% CI 1.0% to 44.8%) based on the corresponding AUC for RO7117418 up to 30 hours (median: 86.3 hour×ng/mL, 95% CI 38.0 to 185) derived from simulation with a representative population (n=500) using the established population PK model. The predicted increased risk of CRS grade ≥2 of 56.3% (95% CI 4.6% to 97.5%) with 5 mg QW FD was in line with the incidence reported clinically (11/18 patients (61%)). Thus, the PK/CRS modeling results suggested a SUD schedule with an initial dose of 2 mg (low CRS grade ≥2 risk with FD), followed by 5 mg 1 week later (moderate CRS grade ≥2 risk with FD).

sec.title: Tissue PD results
sec.p: The aim of tissue PD assessments was to identify mode-of-action-based proximal and distal PD effects downstream of TLR7 activation in tumor tissue. Based on the non-clinical data described above, our hypotheses included (1) the activation of myeloid cells, (2) the induction of immune-stimulatory genes downstream of TLR7, and (3) the potential increase of CD8 T cells in the TME as a distal consequence of the inflammatory modulation of the TME. We performed snRNAseq and CD8 T cell immunohistochemistry analyses on paired liver tumor tissue biopsies collected from 11 patients before and 29 days after the first treatment with 5 mg RO7119929 in the FD expansion cohort. Of these 11 patients, 3 had HCC, 3 had cholangiocarcinoma (2 extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma and 1 intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma), 2 had colorectal cancer, and 1 each had ampullary cancer, pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. Five patients each presented with stable disease or progressive disease as best overall response, and one patient was not evaluable for response.

Figure 5A and online supplemental figure S7 provide an overview of the immune cell composition in the TME assessed via snRNA-seq, with a predominant presence of myeloid leukocytes, and in particular macrophages of an M2-like, immune-suppressive phenotype at baseline (figure 5B, left). We observed a slight, not statistically significant increase in macrophages from a median presence of 70% at baseline to a median of 84% on-treatment across all patients (figure 5B). Administration of RO7119929 induced a significant increase in M1-like, immune-stimulatory-related gene expression, with selected M1-like tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) such as CD300E,13 CXCL10, and CXCL1114 showing a trend for increased expression on treatment. In contrast, we did not observe a clear trend for the modulation of M2-like, immune-suppressive gene expression on treatment. Individual M2-like genes such as MRC215 showed a trend for decreased expression after RO7119929 treatment, while others, such as TREM2,16 did not change consistently across patients, or even showed a slight overall increase on treatment, as exemplified by CD163, which may describe a subpopulation of M2-like TAMs17 (figure 5C, right).

sec.p: Evaluation of genes that are closely associated with downstream TLR7 signaling showed >2-fold induction of the ISGs ISG15, MX1, XAF1, and HERC5 (figure 5D). Furthermore, we observed an RO7119929-induced increase in gene signatures associated with inflammatory signaling. The strongest and statistically significant increases were observed for the type 1 IFN response, viral sensing and immunity, antiviral IFN, and innate antiviral IFN response gene signatures (figure 5E). Increases in the density of tumor-infiltrating CD8 T cells were observed for four patients (range: 1.5-fold to 3.8-fold), while the CD8 T cell density remained unchanged in one patient and decreased in four patients (biopsies of two patients could not be assessed) (figure 5F,G). Subanalysis of proliferating (Ki67+) and non-proliferating (Ki67−) CD8 subsets revealed trends identical to those for total CD8 densities; therefore, in accordance with our validated benchmarking,18 total CD8 density is reported as the primary metric. Interestingly, all increases in CD8 T cell density on treatment were associated with a clinical radiographic response of stable disease (per RECIST V.1.1 criteria) and in three of the four cases with a treatment duration >90 days. Of the five patients with unchanged or decreased CD8 T cell densities, four experienced progressive disease as best overall radiographic response and one stable disease, and all five patients had a treatment duration of <90 days (figure 5G).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The ability of TLR agonists to stimulate innate and adaptive immunity is a promising approach to amplify the response to immunotherapy in combination with CPI mAbs. This study presents our translational and clinical assessment of a novel, oral TLR7 agonist prodrug, RO7119929. As it is converted to the active drug primarily in the liver, we hypothesized that it enhances antitumor activity in malignant liver tumors while diminishing systemic immune activation, which hampers the use of TLR7 agonists for the treatment of cancer.19

Based on the preclinical results demonstrating antitumor activity and the proinflammatory proof-of-mechanism in mice liver tumors and cynomolgus monkey liver tissue, we initiated the first-in-human study of RO7119929 patients with unresectable advanced or metastatic primary liver cancers and other solid tumors with predominant liver involvement. In this study, the TLR7 prodrug showed good oral bioavailability and rapid and complete conversion to the active drug. Peak levels of the oral drug were achieved between 1 and 6 hours after dosing, and the derived effective half-life was 3 hours.

The overall safety profile of RO7119929 QW was manageable up to an FD of 6 mg. No formal MTD could be established. Consistent with the mechanism of action of TLR agonists and published literature,20 our study identified CRS as a key safety risk. Clear reporting guidelines allowed careful evaluation of signs and symptoms as well as the time course of CRS. The incidence and severity of CRS were dose-dependent and the most severe event was generally observed after the first dose. The time course was predictable, and the symptoms generally resolved within 24 hours with routine treatment. The most commonly reported symptoms were fever and chills, as well as hypotension for CRS grade ≥2. Modeling revealed a strong relationship between PK, IL-6, and CRS grade ≥2 after the first dose of RO7119929 and proposed a SUD dosing regimen of 2 mg as first dose (predicted probability of CRS grade ≥2 of 2%) and 5 mg as second dose of RO7119929. Together with updated CRS management guidelines, the SUD approach appeared to reduce the occurrence of severe CRS events and may offer advantages over FD. No CRS grade ≥2 was reported following the 2 mg RO7119929 SUD starting dose and patients receiving SUD experienced less CRS grade ≥2 versus those receiving the comparable target dose as FD (no patient vs 11/18 patients at a target dose of 5 mg, and 2/5 vs 9/10 patients at a target dose of 6 mg).

IL-6-associated CRS is well described for T cell engagers,21 and can be mitigated by a SUD schedule. Attenuation of IL-6 levels after repeat dosing is also described for TLR7 agonists,22 supporting the exploration of both a SUD schedule and tocilizumab (IL-6 receptor blockade) pretreatment with a single dose before initiating TLR7 agonist treatment. Stringent CRS management guidelines (including optional paracetamol pretreatment for subsequent doses) combined with the SUD dosing approach appeared to help mitigate severe CRS events and may have advantages over FD. No conclusion on tocilizumab pretreatment schedule could be drawn, as only one patient had been treated with this dosing schedule at the time the study was terminated.

The patient population enrolled in this study represents a population with a poor prognosis,23 as more than half of the patients presented with liver metastasis and had received at least two prior lines of therapy. This is reflected in the outcome, with the majority of patients with liver metastasis reporting progressive disease as the best overall response. However, one patient with HCC experienced a durable and ongoing complete response to treatment, with additional patients with HCC reporting prolonged disease control. While the effectiveness of cancer immunotherapy is not established in tumor types such as pancreatic cancer and colorectal cancer beyond certain patient subsets such as mismatch repair-deficient/microsatellite instability colorectal cancer,24 25 HCC is known to be responsive to CPI therapy.26,28 We therefore hypothesize that combination therapy with a CPI may further unleash the pro-inflammatory potential of TLR7 agonists and increase antitumor activity, as demonstrated in our preclinical Hep55.1c mouse combination experiment.

Our clinical data align with our own preclinical data presented here and the preclinical and clinical studies reviewed by Rolfo et al20 that TLR7 agonists trigger the reprogramming of the TME towards a proinflammatory phenotype. More specifically, we observed transient, dose-dependent cytokine and ISG increases downstream of TLR7 activation in the peripheral blood. We postulate that the observed treatment-induced changes are due to secondary activation effects via plasmacytoid dendritic cells and other TLR7-expressing myeloid cells rather than direct RO7117418 stimulation. This is supported by modest TLR7 induction in the peripheral blood of treated patients.

The reduced IL-6 levels in the peripheral blood observed during SUD compared with FD are in line with previous reports on SUD regimens for cancer immunotherapy.29 However, these reports generally focus on T cell engagers and the IFN-γ/TNF-α release by activated T cells as the primary inducers of CRS.30 We do not have a complete understanding of the underlying mechanism of retaining IFN-α as well as ISG levels in SUD versus FD of RO7119929 while at the same time seeing a significant reduction in secreted IL-6 levels. One potential hypothesis is that SUD limits the nuclear factor kappa B-mediated primary and also secondary IL-6 production by endothelial cells31 while maintaining the IRF7-mediated IFN-α response of TLR7-positive immune cells.32

Complementing the biological changes in the periphery, our analysis of the TME using paired liver tumor biopsies revealed an increase in immune-stimulatory TLR7-related signals such as ISG, type I IFN, innate and myeloid cell gene induction. Similar to Janku et al,33 we observed a predominant increase in TAM. In line with our preclinical data, snRNA-seq demonstrated a RO7119929/RO7117418-induced shift of this TAM population towards an immune-stimulatory compared with an immune-suppressive phenotype that may be the basis to further boost long-term clinical response in combination with CPI in patients with HCC, as reported by Kim et al.34

Overall, the observed trends in TLR7-related PD modulation of the TME confirmed target engagement and the mode of action of RO7119929 and its active drug RO7117418. However, in line with previous reports,20 the proinflammatory TME resulted only in a moderate CD8 T cell induction. Patients who showed an increase in CD8 tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) reported a clinical benefit (as measured by best overall response of stable disease and treatment duration >90 days) compared with patients with no change or decrease in CD8 TILs. We did not further analyze the liver microenvironment due to the limited total number of evaluable paired biopsies and their origin, which represented a mixture of primary and secondary liver cancers. A more detailed analysis using a homogeneous patient population treated with RO7119929 alone as well as in combination with CPI would be required to better understand the TLR7-mediated effect, with or without CPI, on the TAM phenotypes, CD8 TILs, and tumor cell killing.

In conclusion, while a single durable complete response was observed in a patient with HCC, the overall single-agent clinical activity of RO7119929 was limited in this phase 1 study. Despite the liver-activated mode-of-action of RO7119929, CRS was identified as a dose-limiting risk on initial dosing, with events being dose-dependent and predictable. Novel targeted approaches to administer TLR7 agonists such as immune-stimulating antibody conjugates20 35 combined with careful dose and schedule optimization are eagerly awaited to confirm the potential of TLR agonists as a treatment modality for HCC and other solid tumors.
